History:
- Chief complaint: ~3 weeks of progressive left-sided reduced hearing with persistent left-sided facial numbness (around left ear and along jawline).
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began ~3 weeks ago and have been ongoing; occasional tinnitus (ringing) and intermittent dizziness associated with the ringing.
- Context/triggers/associated symptoms: No ear discharge, no ear pain, no fever. No other body weakness, no swallowing difficulty, no speech or vision problems. Prior remote history of “labyrinthitis” per patient. Symptoms are impacting work (jockey) due to dizziness with ringing.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: Nasal polyps (intermittently symptomatic).
- Remote illness: Patient reports a past diagnosis described as “labyrinthitis” (patient unsure of details).
- Medications: Prescription nasal spray for nasal polyps — name dose/route/frequency not documented; occasional Rennies (antacid) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: Latex.
- Family history: Brother with neurofibromatosis (type not specified).
- Social: Lives with partner; occupation — jockey. Smoking/alcohol not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Reported/observed findings: Persistent left-sided facial numbness present at time of consult; reduced hearing left-sided per patient report; occasional tinnitus and dizziness.
- Relevant negatives recorded during history: No weakness elsewhere, no difficulty swallowing, no speech difficulty, no vision problems, no ear discharge, no ear pain, no fever.
- In-person physical exam/vitals: Not recorded (video consult; clinician requested face-to-face assessment today).

Impression:
- One-line clinical impression: Subacute (≈3 weeks) left-sided hearing loss with ipsilateral facial sensory disturbance — concerning for a peripheral cranial nerve or cerebellopontine angle process; clinician raised Bell’s palsy as a possible diagnosis but further in-person neurological and ear examination is required to clarify.
- DDx consistent with transcript (top considerations):
  - Vestibular schwannoma: justified by unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus and ipsilateral facial sensory symptoms plus family history of neurofibromatosis.
  - Labyrinthitis / vestibular neuritis: supported by prior history and current tinnitus/dizziness, but facial numbness is atypical.
  - Ramsay Hunt syndrome / Bell’s palsy-type process: considered by clinician; absence of documented facial weakness or vesicular rash makes classic presentation less likely.

Management Plan:
- Immediate actions advised:
  - Arrange same-day face-to-face clinic assessment (neurological examination and ear/otoscopic inspection) — clinician has asked admin to book patient into a clinic today.
  - Patient instructed to contact the support team number (to be placed in notes) after five minutes so they can be slotted into a convenient clinic appointment.
  - Preliminary reassurance provided that this does not appear to be imminently life-threatening based on video assessment.
- Pending/conditional actions:
  - Further tests (audiometry and/or neuroimaging) may be required depending on findings of the in-person exam (to be determined at clinic).
- No medications or procedures were prescribed during the video consult.

Patient Summary:
- Mary Richards (40) reports ~3 weeks of worsening left-sided hearing loss with persistent numbness around the left ear/jawline, occasional tinnitus and intermittent dizziness. The clinician suspects a peripheral cranial nerve/ear-related process (Bell’s palsy mentioned as a possibility) but requested an urgent in-person neurological and ear examination today to confirm diagnosis and decide further testing.

Key Takeaways:
- Attend the face-to-face clinic today for neurological and ear examination.
- Call the support team number (placed in notes) after five minutes to be allocated a clinic slot.
- Preliminary reassurance given; further evaluation needed to exclude compressive or other causes.

Next Steps:
- Clinic visit today for focused cranial nerve/neurological exam and otoscopic inspection.
- Based on clinic findings: arrange targeted investigations (e.g., audiometry and/or imaging) if indicated; follow-up with clinician after in-person assessment.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs; objective physical exam findings; formal audiometry results; any ordered imaging; exact name/dose/route/frequency of nasal spray and Rennies; smoking/alcohol history; details/type of family member’s neurofibromatosis.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted (DDx expands on possible causes consistent with the history).
- Transcript quality: Overall clear video consult with some brief inaudible/filler phrases; limited by lack of in-person exam and absence of objective testing.
